COPENHAGEN, Denmark, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Siteimprove, the agentic content intelligence platform, announced today that it is a launch partner for Agentic Commerce on AWS Marketplace, making the Siteimprove.ai Accessibility Agent available for AI agents to pay for per request through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments, with charges in US dollars on the buyer's existing AWS bill.

Siteimprove logo

With Agentic Commerce, AI agents can discover and pay for the Siteimprove.ai Accessibility Agent at the moment they need it, within the spending limits and policies their organization sets. This lets Siteimprove turn each agent request into a monetization event, while buyers keep governance and cost visibility in the tools they already use. This helps digital teams put accessibility checks and fixes to work in their agents faster, with accessibility issues in their content caught and closed as it's created.

Agentic Commerce on AWS Marketplace lets AI agents pay per request for APIs listed by AWS Marketplace sellers through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments, using an extension of the x402 payment protocol. Charges appear in US dollars on the buyer's existing AWS bill, with no crypto wallet required. Builders using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can discover Agentic Commerce listings through AgentCore Gateway. Organizations keep control through spending limits, approved vendor lists, and IAM-based policies. Transactions are limited to verified AWS Marketplace sellers that have completed KYC compliance checks, and charges appear on the buyer's AWS bill with visibility in AWS Cost Explorer and audit records in AWS CloudTrail.

"AI agents are becoming part of how digital teams get work done, and they need trusted insight to do it well. By making the Siteimprove.ai Accessibility Agent available through Agentic Commerce on AWS Marketplace, we let our customers' AI agents get what they need the moment they need it, with the governance their organization requires," said Clay Garrard, CTO, Siteimprove.

The Siteimprove.ai Accessibility Agent is available through Agentic Commerce on AWS Marketplace today. To learn more, visit our page on AWS Marketplace.

About Siteimprove
Founded in 2003, Siteimprove transforms access to the digital world by providing an agentic content intelligence platform that unifies accessibility, analytics, SEO/AEO, and content strategy. Today, global 2000 clients across manufacturing, government, higher education, financial services, and healthcare rely on Siteimprove.ai, an agentic content intelligence platform to deliver both content that performs and that is compliant. Based in Copenhagen, Bellevue, Minneapolis and London, Siteimprove is a single, actionable source of truth for digital content and development teams across many of the largest global enterprises, government entities and learning institutions. Siteimprove is majority-owned by Nordic Capital.

Bloomberg reported on November 13, 2026, that one bank's strategists expect the S&P 500 to reach 8,700 within 12 months. They also see earnings growth slowing to 11% in 2027 from 36% in 2026. That gap matters because slower profit growth changes what investors reward. According to the report, buyers are willing to pay up for companies that keep growing, because growth is becoming harder to find. For stock pickers, that raises the value of any name where earnings momentum is still intact. It matters most when the market has not yet priced all of it in.

Slower Profit Growth Raises the Bar

On November 13, 2026, chip stocks sold off and the S&P 500 fell 0.4%, although it still gained about 2.5% on the week, according to Yahoo Finance's market coverage. Wholesale inflation also reached its highest annual rate in nearly four years, and the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.15% on November 13, 2026. Higher yields make future earnings worth less today. That is one reason the largest technology companies have drawn scrutiny, since their spending has pushed free cash flow negative. Even so, Bloomberg's report described them as "relatively defensive." Readers who want a broader look at the rebound case can see our ranking of oversold AI stocks where Wall Street analysts see big upside.

What a Price Target Really Means

A price target is an analyst's estimate of where a stock should trade in about 12 months, built from forecasts for earnings, growth and a reasonable valuation multiple. Upside is simply the gap between today's share price and the average of those targets, expressed as a percentage. Because targets are opinions rather than guarantees, they can move quickly after a company reports, and a cut does not always mean the analyst has turned negative. Sometimes a firm trims its target to reflect a stock that has already risen, or an expectations bar that was set too high, while keeping a positive rating.

That is why the rating and the target are best read together. An upgrade with a lower target tells a different story from a reiterated rating with a higher one. The reasons behind a change, such as delayed contracts, better cost control or a pricing shift, usually say more than the number does. Ranking by average upside adds a second layer. A large gap to the average target can point to a stock that has fallen out of favor as easily as to one analysts expect to take off. Our list of NYSE-listed stocks with large analyst-estimated upside shows how wide that spread can get on a single exchange. Following the reasons as well as the numbers keeps that distinction clear.

title: Amazon Beat QQQ, But The Ride Was Much Harder
detail:
Amazon Beat QQQ, But The Ride Was Much Harder
Trefis Team

AMZN

ANT
GOOGN
MSFT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Today's big story: Could Anthropic Stock Fall 25%?

Most talk about Amazon.com this week is about its stake in Anthropic. This piece looks at something else. It asks what owning Amazon for ten years was really like.

The answer first. $1 million put into Amazon at the close on Friday, Nov 18, 2016 was worth $7,044,306 at Wednesday's close. That is a gain of 604.4%, or 21.6% a year. The same $1 million in QQQ grew to $6,024,248. QQQ is a fund that tracks the Nasdaq-100 index of large Nasdaq stocks.

The ride was much harder than the ending suggests. Amazon's worst fall took it down 56.1% between July 8, 2021 and Dec 28, 2022. It then needed 694 trading days from the peak to get back to its old high. QQQ, Alphabet and Microsoft each recovered faster from their own worst falls.

What did the 2022 fall do to the stake?

At Amazon's record close on July 8, 2021, the 2016 stake was worth $4,908,717. At the low on Dec 28, 2022, it was worth $2,152,705. The holder gave back $2,756,012 of paper gains. Even so, the stake was still worth more than twice the starting $1 million.

Watching $2,756,012 of gains disappear is hard to sit through. A smaller drop makes it easier to stay invested. Holding on is easier when your portfolio falls less than the market. For every dollar its benchmark lost, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio lost about 81 cents on average. See the HQ record.

The wait was long as well. Amazon did not close above its July 2021 record close again until April 11, 2024. In calendar 2022 alone, the stock returned -49.6%. In calendar 2023 it returned 80.9%.

The stake's lowest dollar value came much earlier. Its lowest close in the ten years was $973,927 on Dec 2, 2016. It sat below the starting $1 million on only 9 trading days, all in the first weeks.

Why did Amazon fall so far in 2022?

Our data does not tie the fall to one cause, so we do not name one. The company's own figures show what the business went through in those years. Revenue still grew, from $469.8 billion in fiscal 2021 to $514.0 billion in fiscal 2022. Operating income, the profit from running the business, fell 50.8% from fiscal 2021 to fiscal 2022.

Fiscal 2022 also ended with a net loss of $2.7 billion. Net income is the profit left after every cost, tax and investment gain or loss. In fiscal 2023, operating income rose to $36.9 billion. By fiscal 2025 it had reached $80.0 billion.

United Parcel Service (NYSE:UPS) has paid $1.64 per share every quarter from the February 18, 2025 ex-dividend date through the latest one on November 16, 2026. That freeze follows years of raises, from $0.91 a quarter in 2018 to $1.63 in 2024. When a long-time raiser stops raising, it is usually protecting cash (a frozen payout and a near-6% yield are two of the seven warning signs we broke down in a free dividend trap guide). At $108.83, the $6.56 annualized payout yields about 6%.

Justin Sullivan / Getty Images
UPS Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.
Free Cash Flow Barely Covers the Check

UPS guides to about $6.1 billion of adjusted free cash flow in 2026 against roughly $5.4 billion in dividends. That works out to about 89% of free cash flow. The 2025 buffer was thinner: $5.470 billion of free cash flow against $5.398 billion in dividends, or roughly 99%. Through nine months of 2026, free cash flow reached $4.2 billion and dividends $4.1 billion.

Earnings coverage is similar. The annual payout equals about 90% of the $7.28 adjusted EPS guidance. Buybacks, which were $1.0 billion in 2025, fell to zero in each 2026 quarter.
